questions.stem: In the particle model, how is every particle of a substance represented?

options.text: As small solid spheres, whatever the substance
options.explanation: The model represents all particles as small solid spheres, whichever state or substance is drawn.

options.text: As cubes for solids, droplets for liquids and dots for gases
options.explanation: The model uses the same spheres throughout; only their arrangement and spacing change.

options.text: As atoms for elements but molecules for compounds
options.explanation: The simple model draws every particle the same way and does not separate particle types.

options.text: As large spheres in solids and tiny ones in gases
options.explanation: Particle size stays fixed; spacing and arrangement carry the differences between states.

questions.stem: How do the particles of a solid move?

options.text: They vibrate about fixed positions
options.explanation: A regular arrangement holds each particle in place, so solids only vibrate on the spot.

options.text: They slide around each other freely
options.explanation: Moving around each other describes liquid particles, not the fixed sites of a solid.

options.text: They move quickly in all directions
options.explanation: Fast motion in all directions belongs to gas particles, which are also far apart.

options.text: They stay completely still at all temperatures
options.explanation: Solid particles always vibrate, and the vibration grows as more energy is supplied.

questions.stem: Which description matches the particles of a gas?

options.text: Randomly arranged, far apart and moving quickly in all directions
options.explanation: The properties table gives gases random arrangement, wide spacing and fast movement in all directions.

options.text: Regularly arranged and vibrating about fixed positions
options.explanation: That is the solid row of the table, not the gas row.

options.text: Randomly arranged, close together and moving around each other
options.explanation: That is the liquid row; gas particles are far apart rather than close.

options.text: Regularly arranged, far apart and almost still
options.explanation: Gases are random rather than regular, and their particles move quickly.

questions.stem: At what temperature does a pure substance melt, and at what temperature does it freeze?

options.text: At the same temperature: the melting point of the substance
options.explanation: Melting and freezing both take place at the melting point, which is why the two changes share one temperature.

options.text: Melting needs a higher temperature than freezing
options.explanation: Both changes occur at the single melting-point temperature for a pure substance.

options.text: Both occur at the boiling point
options.explanation: The boiling point is where liquid and gas interconvert, not where solid and liquid do.

options.text: At whatever temperature the change happens to be observed
options.explanation: State changes occur at fixed temperatures that are properties of the substance.

questions.stem: How does the spacing of liquid particles compare with that of solid particles?

options.text: Both are close, but solid particles are in a regular arrangement while liquid particles are random
options.explanation: Solids are very close and regular; liquids remain close but lose the ordered pattern.

options.text: Liquid particles are far apart while solid particles are packed together
options.explanation: Being far apart describes gases; liquid particles stay close to one another.

options.text: Solid particles sit further apart than liquid particles
options.explanation: The solid is the most tightly packed state of the three.

options.text: Neither state keeps its particles close together
options.explanation: Both solids and liquids keep particles close; only gases spread them far apart.

questions.stem: What is the difference between boiling and evaporation?

options.text: Boiling happens throughout the liquid at one fixed temperature; evaporation happens only at the surface across a range of temperatures
options.explanation: Bubbles form inside the liquid at the boiling point, while high-energy particles escape from the surface below it.

options.text: Boiling happens at the surface while evaporation forms bubbles inside the liquid
options.explanation: It is the reverse: bubbles form inside during boiling, and evaporation is a surface process.

options.text: They are identical processes that simply carry different names
options.explanation: Both the temperature range and the location within the liquid differ between them.

options.text: Evaporation needs a higher temperature than boiling
options.explanation: Evaporation can occur at temperatures below the boiling point, not above some higher threshold.

questions.stem: A pure liquid is frozen until it solidifies. How does the temperature at which it freezes compare with the temperature at which the same liquid melts?

options.text: At exactly the same temperature
options.explanation: Freezing is the reverse of melting and happens at the same temperature, as with water at 0 °C.

options.text: At a lower temperature than melting
options.explanation: The melting point and freezing point of a pure substance are one and the same value.

options.text: At a higher temperature than melting
options.explanation: No gap separates the two; they coincide at the melting point.

options.text: Freezing has no fixed temperature at all
options.explanation: Freezing occurs at a specific temperature once enough thermal energy is lost.

questions.stem: Why does melting count as a physical change rather than a chemical one?

options.text: Because the particles themselves stay the same and only the forces between them change
options.explanation: The particles remain unchanged throughout; it is only the forces between them that alter.

options.text: Because a new chemical substance forms each time the state changes
options.explanation: No new substance appears: water is water whether ice, liquid or steam.

options.text: Because the particles are broken apart and remade in a new form
options.explanation: Particles persist throughout the change; only their arrangement and energy differ afterwards.

options.text: Because no energy is ever taken in or given out
options.explanation: Energy is central: it is absorbed to overcome forces and released as particles settle.

questions.stem: How does the strength of the forces between particles affect the melting and boiling points of a substance?

options.text: Stronger forces need more energy to overcome, so both points are higher
options.explanation: More energy is needed to overcome stronger forces, which raises the melting and boiling points.

options.text: Stronger forces make the points lower because particles hold together less
options.explanation: Holding together more strongly demands more energy to separate, which raises the points.

options.text: Force strength has no effect on either point
options.explanation: The energy needed to change state depends directly on how strong the forces are.

options.text: Only the boiling point responds to force strength
options.explanation: Both the melting point and the boiling point rise when forces are stronger.

options.text: A solid changes directly into a gas, as iodine and solid carbon dioxide do
options.explanation: Sublimation is the direct solid-to-gas change, shown by only a few solids such as iodine and solid carbon dioxide.

options.text: Any solid can be made to sublime if enough heat is supplied
options.explanation: Only a few solids, such as iodine or solid carbon dioxide, behave this way.

options.text: A liquid changes into a solid as it cools
options.explanation: That change is freezing, the reverse of melting.

options.text: A gas changes directly into a solid as it cools
options.explanation: That direction is deposition or desublimation, the reverse of sublimation.
